To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The vanA, vanC and vanB gene clusters are not the source for vancomycin resistance in Enterococcus casselflavus/flavscens, Enterococcus gallinaram, Lactobaccillus spp., Erysipelothric rhusiopathae, and Leuconostc spp. and Pediococcus sp. However
the glycopeptide resistance-associated gene clusters in non-enterococcus bacteria are not the origin of the vancomycin resistance in enterococcal bacteria.

the glycopeptide resistance gene clusters of Enterococcus faecalis, E. faecium and Enterococcus galliarum are not identical, and that there are organisms other than enterococci that contain genes homologous to those found in enterococcal glycopeptide resistance clusters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular epidemiology and evolution of vancomycin resistance in enterococcal species.
the molecular mechanisms of glycopeptide resistance in non-enterococcus bacteria, and the origins of the vancomycin resistance gene clusters.
the origins of the vancomycin resistance gene clusters and the dissemination of these gene clusters among enterococci, and among non-enterococci.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the origins of the glycopeptide resistance-associated genes in non-entercococcal organisms remain unclear.
the vancomycin resistance in enterococcal species has not been acquired from any other bacterial species.
the enterococci have acquired the vancomycin resistance determinants from the environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not able to find the origins of the glycopeptide resistance gene clusters in Enterococcus spp.
the enterococci do not appear to be the source of the glycopeptide resistance-associated genes in other non-enterococci, but rather that there may be other, as yet unidentified, sources.

the vancomycin resistance determinants in enterococcal-type organisms are likely to have been acquired from environmental sources, and that the glycopeptide resistance determinants of the enterococcus are likely to have originated from a non-enterococci source.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there are many organisms that have genes that are homologous to those in the glycopeptide resistance gene clusters of enterococci; however, these organisms do not necessarily harbor glycopeptide resistance.
the vancomycin resistance determinants in enterococcal isolates from humans and livestock are not the result of horizontal transfer of resistance from non-enterococci.
glycopeptide resistance is not a rare phenomenon, but rather a ubiquitous characteristic of many bacteria.
